text: Elena was eight, and her class project was about teeth. She sat on the sofa with her mum's phone and said, "My tooth feels wiggly. I think the dentist should look at it." The phone asked which day she liked. "After school, when it's not raining," said Elena. The assistant found a free time at Dr. Rao's office on Thursday at four and booked it. The screen was very bright, and Elena squinted. "It's so bright in here," she said. The assistant dimmed the screen a little. Elena smiled. "That's fine," she said. The assistant read the booking back to her: Thursday, four o'clock, Dr. Rao. It also set a reminder for Thursday morning so she would not forget. Elena wrote the date on her project poster with a big green pen.

A nurse, home from a swim, wants the phone screen to be less bright.
make the screen dimmer
turn down the brightness
pls lower the brigthness
my eyes hurt, the screen is blinding me
Can you make the display a bit softer?
It's way too bright in here for my phone
Brightness down please
Could you please lower the screen brightness, because I'm lying in bed and my husband is trying to sleep?

A campsite booking is how you keep a spot for your tent. It makes sure there is room when you arrive, so you do not drive for hours and find a full field. People change a booking a lot. They say things like "move it to Saturday," "add one more night," or "make it for five people instead of four." Many sites ask you to pay when you book, and some let you pay when you get there. After a long walk, the best part is often a crispy breakfast cooked on a small stove outside the tent. If the weather turns bad, you can ask to cancel or to switch to another weekend.

Person: Can you book me a haircut and remind me the day before?
Assistant: Of course. Which day would you like the haircut?
Person: Friday morning, after I lock up the greenhouse.
Assistant: Is nine o'clock all right?
Person: Yes, nine is good. I want a soft trim, nothing short.
Assistant: Done. You are booked for Friday at nine, and I will remind you on Thursday.
Person: Can you also invite my brother and tell him the time?
Assistant: I'm sorry, I can't send invitations to other people. I can book a second chair next to yours, if you like.

name: check_room_air
does: Scans a room for dust, smoke and stale air and says whether the air is smooth and fresh or stuffy.
inputs: which room, and the month if the person wants a pollen check, like April
people say:
- Does it smell stuffy in here?
- Is the air okay in the bedroom?
- My nose is itchy, is it the dust?
- How is the air in the kitchen after cooking?
- Should I open a window?

Reading text aloud is a feature that lets a phone speak the words on its screen. It helps people who find small print hard to see, and people who just want to listen while their hands are busy. Changing it takes quick, simple words. People say "read this to me," "talk slower," "make the text bigger," or "stop reading." Some want a different voice, and some want the phone to look at a page and read it all the way to the end. The length of the text does not matter much, because a short note and a long article both work. You can also ask it to read only one paragraph.

Meera was chopping onions in the noisy kitchen of the restaurant when her phone buzzed on the shelf. She wiped her hands and said, "Tell me if my parcel came today and remind me to pick it up from the post office on my break." The assistant checked the mail notice. It said the parcel was waiting at the post office on Elm Street. Then it set a reminder for two o'clock, which was when her break started. Meera also asked if the delivery date would change, and the assistant said it had not. "Thank you," said Meera. She turned the fan down so she could hear the reminder later and went back to her onions.

Ngozi had moved to the city in june, a few weeks after her baby Ada was born. A neighbour had lent her a baby monitor, but Ngozi had not learned how to turn it on. It was late, and she was holding Ada with one arm, so she typed with her thumb: "remnid me to feed ada in half an hour and put the monitor on". The assistant set a timer for thirty minutes. Then it switched on the monitor in the nursery and told her the sound was working. Ngozi sat down in the dark with Ada and watched the little green light on the phone. When the timer rang, she was ready.

Person: I'm having a party on Saturday and I need music.
Assistant: Nice! What kind of music do you want?
Person: Something perfect for dancing. Not too slow.
Assistant: Okay. How many songs should I put in the playlist?
Person: Double what I had last time. I wrote it down with a pen, but I lost the paper. I think it was thirty.
Assistant: Then I will make it sixty songs. Do you want the volume to rise as the guests arrive?
Person: Yes, can you make it rise slowly?
Assistant: I'm sorry, I can't change the volume on a schedule. I can start the playlist quietly, and you can turn it up when the room fills.

Eun-ji woke up on Saturday with a jump. Her sister's birthday dinner was that night, and she had no gift. She grabbed her phone from the pillow, still half asleep, and said, "Gift ideas." The assistant asked who the gift was for. "My sister. She likes plants," said Eun-ji. The assistant gave three ideas: a small fern, a fancy watering can and a book about herbs. Eun-ji liked the watering can. Then she asked the assistant to put "buy a card" on her list for the afternoon. She told no one about the plan, so the secret did not leak, and at the dinner her sister was the only guest who was surprised.

Omar had moved to the city a week ago and knew almost nobody. One night he lay in bed, tired, with a book on his phone. He said, "Could you please play my audiobook from where I stopped? I fell asleep last night, and I missed the end of the chapter." The assistant found his place in chapter nine and began to play. The story was about a girl on a long swim across a cold lake. The screen was bright, so Omar asked the assistant to dim it, and it lowered the light. The narrator's voice felt close and calm in the quiet room. When Omar stopped answering, the assistant paused the book and saved his place.

Lucy sat in her kitchen with her phone on the table. Her granddaughter lived in Switzerland, where it was snowy, and Lucy wanted to send her a rose bouquet from a shop there. "How much is a hundred francs in dollars?" she asked. Then she laughed. "Oh, no. I meant pounds, not dollars. I live in England, I don't know why I said dollars." The assistant looked up the exchange rate and said that a hundred francs was a little less than a hundred pounds. Lucy wrote the number on a note. "Remember the rate for me, please," she said, and the assistant saved it to her notes before she went to order the flowers.

name: quiet_sender
does: Stops mail from a frequent sender from landing in the inbox and drops it into a folder instead.
inputs: the sender's name or address (it could be a husband, a shop or a club), and the folder
people say:
- Stop the shop emails from showing up in my inbox
- I get too many mails from the gym
- Send everything from Pedro to the newsletter folder
- Those daily deals are driving me crazy
- Can you hide emails from that club?

name: plan_walk_route
does: Plans a walk or run of the right length and tells you if it is going to snow, so you do not get bored of the same old loop.
inputs: where to start (like the train station), and how long or how far
people say:
- I want a different run today
- Somewhere new to walk, thirty minutes
- The same loop is boring me
- A route from the station that is about five kilometres
- Where can I go for a walk with the dog?

Nora sat at her desk with a cold coffee in one hand. Her video call kept freezing, and her boss was talking about the end of the quarter. She typed with her other hand: "wifi is so slwo, can you restart the router". The assistant said it would restart the router, and it did. The little lights on the box went dark and then came back one by one. After about a minute, the assistant told her the wifi was working again. Nora tried the call again, and this time the picture stayed sharp. It was fast enough for her boss's slides to load without any stops. She thanked the assistant and finished the meeting.

Mariam got home from the hospital at seven in the morning after a long night shift. She was cold and tired. She carried a bag of groceries into the kitchen and put down a bottle of orange juice. "Tonight after dinner, make my bedroom warmer by several degrees," she said to the thermostat. The assistant asked how warm she wanted it. "About twenty-one," said Mariam. The assistant set the heating for the evening, and it turned the radiator in the hall down so no heat was wasted. Then Mariam drank her juice, drew the curtains and slept all day. When she woke up, the bedroom was nice and warm.

Person: I forgot how tall I am in feet. I am 140.
Assistant: 140 what? Centimetres?
Person: Yes, centimetres.
Assistant: That is about four feet seven.
Person: Is a cow taller than me?
Assistant: A cow is usually about 140 to 150 centimetres tall at the shoulder. So it is about the same as you, or a little more.
Person: Wow. Thank you!
Assistant: You're welcome. It was nice of you to ask so politely, and I hope the farm trip is fun.

A world clock tells you what time it is in other cities. It is for people who call family far away or who work with teams in different places. Before a call, you might say "what time is it in Tokyo?" or "is it too late to ring Mum in Lima?" People also change the clock itself: "add Sydney," "show me London and Cairo," or "move my alarm back one hour." A rough rule is that each step across the map is about an hour. If you want to schedule a meeting, check that the hour works for everyone. Mail in a mailbox is collected at local time, and calls are too.

Beatrice was cooking beans on the stove when hot water splashed onto her hand. It hurt, but her roommates were asleep, so she whispered to her phone, "My hand got burned. I don't want a long video, just tell me what to do." The assistant answered in a quiet voice. It told her to hold the burn under cool running water for ten minutes. It said not to use ice, butter or toothpaste. Then it asked if the skin had blisters, and she said no. The assistant told her to cover the burn with a clean cloth and to call a doctor if it got worse. Beatrice turned off the stove and held her hand under the tap.

Haruto was seventy-two and needed a new switch for the lamp in his hall. He sat with his tablet and said, "I want to order a light switch, a plain white one, and have it come on the first of May." The assistant showed him three switches. One was very expensive, with a little screen on it, and Haruto laughed. He picked the cheapest white one. The assistant ordered it and chose the first of May for delivery. It also reminded him to disconnect the power at the main box before changing the old switch. Haruto wrote "turn off the power first" on a sticky note and put it on the lamp.

Sabine had taught maths for forty years, and now she was in her kitchen waiting for her grandchildren. The shop had shipped her a new router last week, but the old wifi still kept dropping with constant stops. She typed with two fingers, fast and without capitals: "guest wifi pasword for the kids". The assistant made a guest network with a short password and read it out slowly: two words and four numbers. It also said that the guests could not see her files. Sabine wrote the password on a card and put it on the fridge. When the children arrived, they connected in a minute, and Sabine made tea.

Text messages are short notes you send from one phone to another. A group chat is a text with many people in it, like a family planning a pizza night. People use texts to ask questions, share photos and reply later when they are busy. To change how texts work, they say things like "read my messages," "reply that I'm on my way," "mute this chat," or "send the first one again." If the order needs a total, someone might type "how much is it all together?" Some phones read new messages aloud, which helps when your hands are full, and they let you answer by talking.

Thu was a cook, and guests were coming to her flat in an hour. She was in the kitchen, stirring a pot, when she remembered that she had lost her necklace behind the sofa. "In an hour my friends come," she said to the speaker. "Make the living room lights brighter, and tell me when it is half past six." The assistant raised the ceiling lights to full. Thu found the necklace under a cushion and laughed. Then she asked for warmer light, because the white glare did not show the true colour of the food. The assistant changed the lamps to a soft yellow, and she was happy. She still had time to vacuum the rug.

Bjorn was sixteen and texting his friends in the family room when he noticed the electricity bill on the table. It looked high. He picked up his phone and typed, "How much less power did we use this month than last month?" The assistant looked at the home energy numbers and said they had used about half as much as in winter, thanks to the new solar panels. Bjorn was happy. "Post a picture of that graph in the family chat," he said, and the assistant did. Then he put his dad's hammer back in the drawer, since he had been fixing the bike earlier, and went to eat dinner.

A video is a moving picture that you record on your phone and watch later. People use videos to remember things, like a trip to visit grandparents or a clip of a cat chasing an orange across the kitchen. After you record a clip, you can share it with a friend or send it to a family chat. People change things with short requests: "trim the end," "make it shorter," "play it again," "send this to Dad," or "save it to my phone." If something is urgent, such as a clip that must reach someone before a deadline, they say "send it now."

Score?

name: camp_night_check
does: Says how cold the night will get at a campsite, based on the recent weather and the expected fall in temperature, so campers know what to pack if the air will chill.
inputs: the campsite or place, the date, and how high up it is
people say:

- Do I need a thicker sleeping bag?

- Should I bring a warm jacket for the hills?
- What's the weather like for our tent trip this weekend?

Baking bread takes time, and the oven timer helps. The dough must rise first, and then it bakes. People set the timer and change it with short requests: "ten more minutes," "make it fifteen," or "turn the heat down." To check a cake, you push a thin stick into the middle. If it comes out clean, the cake is done. If the top is getting dark too fast, you close the oven door and lower the heat. A busy driver who bakes late at night might say "remind me when the bread is done," because the timer is the only thing keeping the loaf from burning.

A short video can show how to do a small job at home, like how to change a toothbrush head. People also record clips when something good happens: a baby's first steps, a dog that comes running, or a quick tour of a new flat. They watch them later on a phone or a television. To change what a video does, they say "pause," "go back ten seconds," "turn on the words," or "make it louder." When the family gets back from a trip, they often say "play the clips from the beach" or "share the video with Grandma." Home videos are mostly for keeping memories.

name: order_takeaway
does: Orders food from a restaurant and sends it to your door, so nobody has to lose an evening in a queue.
inputs: the restaurant (like the noodle place up the hill), the dishes, and the home address
people say:
- Get me the usual from the Thai place
- I'm too tired to cook, order something

- Dinner for four, delivered by seven
- Can you get that burger place to bring food here?

Person: My room smells funny.
Assistant: I can help. Which room do you mean?
Person: My bedroom. It smells like smoke because Mum burned something in the oven.
Assistant: Okay. Do you want me to scan the air first?
Person: Yes, please.
Assistant: The air is a bit smoky. How long should I run the purifier?
Person: Four hours? It's late and I want to sleep.
Assistant: I will run it for four hours on a low, quiet setting. Please keep your door closed so the air stays clean.

name: wind_down_bedtime

inputs: the bedtime, who it is for, and how many minutes it should last
people say:

- It's late, time for bed for everyone

Time zones are the reason a podcast you love can come out at a different hour for you than for the host. When it is noon where you live, it may be night in another country. A clock app shows these differences, and people use it to check the time before a personal call. They say "what time is it in Berlin?" or "show me Delhi next to my city," or "wake me at eight, my time." When you travel, the phone usually changes to the new zone on its own. If it looks wrong, you can say "set my clock to local time." A short report of the time is often all you need.

Number of boxes for a two-bedroom place?

An inbox is the place where new emails land. People use it for letters from work, shops and friends. A busy inbox gets messy, so people ask for small changes: "show me only unread mail," "move this to the trip folder," "delete the old ones," or "attach the photo." If a message is about an expensive purchase, they may say "mark it important." Sometimes a short email is not the best way, so people text instead. But long details, like a trip plan with times and addresses, fit better in an email, because they stay in one place and can be found later.

Anil had taught history for thirty years, and now he sat in a restaurant with old friends. The dinner was cooked and nearly ready, but he saw that his everyday account was low. He leaned over his phone and said, "Excuse me, could you please move a hundred pounds from my savings to my checking account? I'd like to pay the bill for everyone tonight." The assistant asked him to confirm. "Yes, a hundred," he said. It checked the setting for transfers between his own accounts, moved the money, and told him the new balance. Anil guessed the bill would be eighty, and he was right.

people say:

- What's a good hike with a view?

Sylvie had a long day at the office, and her coffee was stale on the desk. She plugged in her laptop and said to her phone, "Move my meeting with Tom to Tuesday at two. No, wait, Wednesday at two." The assistant moved the meeting to Wednesday and sent Tom a note about the new time. Then Sylvie remembered the slides. "Upload the slides to the meeting too," she said. The assistant attached the file to the calendar event so everyone could open it. Sylvie checked the screen. Wednesday at two, with the slides. She nodded, finished her cold coffee and went home.

Hodan drove a taxi, and on Wednesday his shift would begin at six. He was hungry and had only a few minutes at the red light. He said to his phone, "Order a chicken wrap from the place on Main Street. No, make that the falafel wrap." The assistant changed the order to a falafel wrap. It asked if he wanted the flat bread or the regular one, and Hodan said flat. The assistant set the delivery for half past five, at his front door. Then it asked about a tip, and he chose ten percent. When the light turned green, Hodan drove on, happy that dinner was coming.

Mia was at a cafe with her friends, and she had written the party plans on a napkin. Her friend Zoe had passed her exams, and they wanted to celebrate. Mia said to her phone, "Text Zoe that we are meeting at six at the pizza place. Don't put any emojis in it, please." The assistant wrote the message with no pictures, only words, and showed it to Mia. She read it, then asked to add "bring your sister." The assistant added the line at the bottom of the message and sent it. Zoe replied right away. Mia put the napkin in her pocket.
